html:
The Kingdom of Mapungubwe was a state in the Limpopo valley, where South Africa, Botswana and Zimbabwe now meet, which flourished from about 1075 to 1220 and is seen as the first kingdom in southern Africa.

Its rulers lived on top of Mapungubwe hill, apart from the commoners below, a sign of a new class divide. They grew rich from trading gold and ivory to the Indian Ocean coast, through ports such as Sofala, for glass beads and cloth. Royal graves on the hill held gold objects, among them the golden rhinoceros.

The state declined in the 13th century, perhaps because of a cooler, drier climate, and power moved north to Great Zimbabwe. Its finds were hidden for decades under apartheid, which denied that Africans had built states. UNESCO listed the site in 2003.
